extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of the history of mathematics; readers of a critical edition/introduction to Archimedes
extracted.subtask_description: An academic introduction surveying Archimedes' relation to his predecessors: which methods he used or assumed, earlier results he cites, and the classical propositions about conics and solid geometry that underlie his work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of traditional geometrical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main methods underlying Greek geometrical algebra are (1) the use of the theory of proportions and (2) the method of application of areas; both are fully expounded in Euclid, though the latter is the older and is used extensively by Apollonius and to a lesser extent by Archimedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that Archimedes often expresses conic properties as proportions rather than by application-of-areas equations; notes relative frequency of each method in Archimedes vs Apollonius and gives examples from Archimedes' texts (e.g. treatment of central conics, on Conoids and Spheroids Props. 2, 25, 26, 29).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of application of areas (application of a rectangle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometric device 'apply a rectangle' to a given straight line equal to a given area, sometimes 'exceeding by a square figure' or 'falling short by a square figure', used to represent and solve quadratic relations geometrically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives specific occurrences in Archimedes (e.g. On the equilibrium of Planes, Prop. 1; On Conoids and Spheroids Props. 2, 25, 26, 29), explains how Archimedes avoids certain forms (he avoids 'falling short by a square' in some cases) and substitutes more complicated constructions to represent x·a, with algebraic equivalence shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of proportions / geometrical algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's theory of proportions (Books V and VI) enabled addition, subtraction, composition (multiplication) and transformation of ratios, effectively providing an algebraic toolkit for magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how addition/subtraction of ratios is effected by bringing to a common denominator (geometrical procedure), and composition/multiplication of ratios can be extended; includes illustrative reductions (e.g. reduction of ratio between cubes to a ratio of straight lines, manipulation of continued proportion series) and concrete examples from Archimedes' propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of auxiliary fixed lines / elimination in proportional methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of auxiliary fixed lines or fixed points in figures to simplify ratios and allow elimination of variables, reducing multi-relation problems to a single equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: On the Sphere and Cylinder, Prop. 4 reduces three relations connecting three undetermined points to one equation by eliminating two points; similar eliminations used in other propositions to manage complicated proportional relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma on unequal magnitudes (equimultiples / exhaustion lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes states: 'Of unequal lines, unequal surfaces, or unequal solids, the greater exceeds the less by such a magnitude as is capable, if added [continually] to itself, of exceeding any given magnitude of those which are comparable with one another.' Euclid's related lemma (Book X or Book V def. leading to x.1) is also central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma underlies proofs by exhaustion (e.g. Euclid xii.2 and Archimedes' use in quadrature/cubature). The text contrasts Archimedes' stated lemma with Euclid's lemma used in the formal proofs, and explains how the lemmas are applied to equilateral polygons inscribed in circles/sectors and to volume proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eudoxus theorems used by Archimedes
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Any pyramid is one third part of the prism with same base and equal height. (2) Any cone is one third part of the cylinder with same base and equal height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes attributes these theorems to Eudoxus and notes that both (especially (1)) are used in his quadrature/cubature results; explains their role in deriving volume ratios via exhaustion and related Euclidean propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other classical solid-geometry propositions assumed
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of propositions Archimedes quotes as earlier results: (3) Cones of equal height are in ratio of their bases; (4) If a cylinder be divided by a plane parallel to the base, cylinder is to cylinder as axis to axis; (5) Cones with same bases and equal height are to one another as the cylinders; (6) Bases of equal cones are reciprocally proportional to their heights; (7) Cones whose base diameters are in the same ratio as their axes are in the triplicate ratio of the diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes these are essentially in Euclid's twelfth Book (with (5) deduced from (2)); explains how they are proved via the method of exhaustion and similarity/completion arguments sketched in the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola properties known prior to Archimedes
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties quoted as proved in the elements of conics: (a) If PV is the diameter of a segment and PVq the chord parallel to the tangent at P, then YV = Vq; (b) if the tangent at P meets VP produced in T, then ... (text: 'ey he' in fragment) ; (c) relations when two chords parallel to tangent meet diameter PV in V, V'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that several fundamental parabola relations (including PV^2 = p·AV etc.) were already well known and used (Menaechmus noted for duplication of the cube); these properties are invoked in Archimedes' quadrature and other constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General conic property: rectangles of intersecting chords vs squares on parallel tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: If straight lines drawn from the same point touch any conic and if two chords parallel to the respective tangents intersect, then the rectangles under the segments of the chords are to one another as the squares on the parallel tangents respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted as 'proved in the conics' and used repeatedly by Archimedes (e.g. in proving nature of plane sections of conicoids and in Props. 3 and 12–14 of On Conoids and Spheroids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola parameter relation (On Conoids and Spheroids, Prop. 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabola with parameter p, given a chord QQ' bisected in I by diameter PV and p the parameter of ordinates to PV, with QD perpendicular to PV, then OV^2 : OD^2 = p : p_a  (text gives OV? 3 OD = p: pa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in volume/section calculations (the treatise references Prop. 3); ties the parameter p to relationships between ordinates and chord segments in sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse properties assumed from earlier conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples stated as known in the conics: PN^2 : AN·A'N = P'N^2 : AN'·A'N' = CB^2 : CA'^2, and OV^2 : PV^2 = OV' : RS : (text gives variants) — properties relating segments, rectangles and ratios in ellipses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes these can be derived from the intersecting-chords/tangent-rectangle property; cited to justify Archimedes' use of ellipse relations in spheroid/conoid propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola properties assumed
rubrics_metrics.description: Stated results: AN·PAW · 2 Vie PANN ... (textual fragments) and OW^2 : PY·OP (relations among segments); specific property: in a hyperbola, if P is any point and PA, PL are drawn parallel to one asymptote and meeting the other, then PK·PL = (constant). Rectangular hyperbola cases known to Menaechmus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentions limits in ancient conception (absence of double hyperbola as single curve hindered some equalities), suggests that subnormal property of parabola and certain harmonic properties in hyperbola may have been known before Archimedes; these are used tacitly in On Floating Bodies and other works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surfaces of the second degree — plane-section properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes' Prop. 11 (On Conoids and Spheroids) asserts: (1) In a paraboloid of revolution any plane section parallel to the axis is a parabola equal to the generating parabola. (2) In a hyperboloid of revolution any plane section parallel to the axis is a hyperbola similar to the generating hyperbola. (3) In a hyperboloid of revolution a plane section through the vertex of the enveloping cone is a hyperbola not similar to the generating hyperbola. (4) In any spheroid a plane section parallel to the axis is an ellipse similar to the generating ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction supplies geometric proofs/sketches: reduce to plane sections through the axis, use properties of intersecting chords and parallels, and show constancy or similarity of the resulting conic; discusses why some hyperbolic sections are not similar (inequalities in derived ratios).
